procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated in the provided text, but implied to be a lower court since the High Court heard an appeal.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 23.03.2015 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Criminal Appeal No. 221 of 2009.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Bombay heard Criminal Appeal No. 221 of 2009 and issued a Judgment and Order dated 23.03.2015. The text indicates the High Court imposed a conviction, which was appealed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Five accused persons filed special leave petitions to appeal the conviction imposed by the High Court. Leave to appeal was granted to these accused. The Supreme Court is hearing five appeals (Criminal Appeal No. 1301 of 2015 and four others) together because the facts are related and the issue involved is connected.

decision.conviction_status: Conviction against Accused Nos. 2 and 3 is set aside. Conviction under Section 302, IPC with respect to Accused No. 1 is maintained. Conviction under Section 307 read with 34, IPC with respect to accused Nos. 5 and 6 is maintained.
decision.sentence_status: Sentence against Accused Nos. 2 and 3 is set aside. Sentence under Section 302, IPC with respect to Accused No. 1 is maintained. Sentence under Section 307 read with 34, IPC with respect to accused Nos. 5 and 6 is maintained.
directions: The concerned authorities are directed to set free Accused Nos. 2 and 3 forthwith, if not required in any other offence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of Accused No. 1 under Section 302 of the IPC is sustainable.

facts: The court distinguished the evidence against Accused No. 1 (A-1) from the evidence against Accused Nos. 2 and 3 (A-2 and A-3).
Weapons were recovered from Accused No. 1, but not from A-2 and A-3.
The court found the evidence against A-2 and A-3 was weak, consisting only of uncorroborated oral testimony with no other supporting evidence like blood stains or weapon recovery.
law: The prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt.
A conviction cannot be based on suspicion or a mere preponderance of probability.
application: The court analyzed the evidence against each accused individually.
It found that while the prosecution failed to prove the case against A-2 and A-3 beyond a reasonable doubt, the same was not true for the other accused.
The court determined that the role of Accused No. 1 was "proved with cogent evidence available on record," which included the recovery of a weapon.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the conviction of Accused No. 1 under Section 302 of the IPC was sustainable because, unlike the case against the acquitted co-accused, his role in the crime was established by cogent evidence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction against Accused Nos. 2 and 3 is sustainable.

facts: The deceased's initial statement to the police did not name Accused Nos. 2 and 3.
No weapons were recovered from Accused Nos. 2 and 3.
An expert opinion revealed that there were no blood stains on the clothes of Accused Nos. 2 and 3.
The only evidence connecting Accused Nos. 2 and 3 to the crime was the oral testimony of a single witness, PW-2.
PW-2's testimony was not independently corroborated; he did not attribute any specific weapon to them, and another witness (PW-11) did not attribute any overt acts to them.
The court noted that the presence of the accused at the police station immediately after the incident, coupled with the lack of evidence, created suspicion about their involvement.
law: The prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt.
An accused has a right not to be convicted unless the offence is established by the standard of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
A court is not permitted to convict an accused based on suspicion or a preponderance of probability.
Oral testimony without independent corroboration cannot be the sole basis for a conviction.
application: The Court found that the prosecution's case against Accused Nos. 2 and 3 rested solely on the uncorroborated oral testimony of witness PW-2.

This testimony was significantly weakened by the lack of any supporting evidence. Specifically, the accused were not named in the deceased's initial statement, no weapons were found, and their clothes had no blood stains.
The Court reasoned that this lack of corroborating evidence meant the prosecution had failed to meet the high standard of proof required in criminal law.
The Court held that the lower courts were wrong to convict based on this insufficient evidence, which at best only raised suspicion rather than proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case against Accused Nos. 2 and 3 beyond a reasonable doubt. Consequently, the Court rejected the sustainability of their conviction and set it aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of Accused Nos. 5 and 6 under Section 307 read with Section 34 of the IPC is sustainable.

facts: Accused Nos. 5 and 6 were named in the First Information Report (FIR) and in an alleged oral declaration by the deceased.
Weapons were recovered from Accused Nos. 5 and 6.
The evidence of the doctor and the injuries sustained by the deceased were considered by the court.
law: The standard of proof required for a criminal conviction is "beyond reasonable doubt".
A conviction must be supported by "cogent evidence" on the record.
application: The Court distinguished the case against Accused Nos. 5 and 6 from that of Accused Nos. 2 and 3, against whom the case was not established beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Court found that the roles of Accused Nos. 5 and 6 were proven with cogent evidence.
The combination of being named in the FIR and the deceased's declaration, along with the medical evidence and recovery of weapons, was sufficient to establish their guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution had successfully established the involvement and guilt of Accused Nos. 5 and 6 beyond a reasonable doubt. Therefore, it upheld their conviction and sentence under Section 307 read with Section 34 of the IPC.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of Accused No. 1 under Section 302 of the IPC is sustainable.
appellant_arguments: The trial court erred in distinguishing the overt acts attributed to the various accused based on the evidence of PW-2.
The evidence of P.W.2 cannot be believed due to contradictions between his statement in the FIR and his evidence in court.
P.W.2 did not attribute an individual role to the accused on the day of the incident.
respondent_arguments: The statements of prosecution witnesses are consistent and point to the guilt of the accused.
The contradictions in the evidence are trivial in nature and do not affect the prosecution's case.
The evidence of the doctor and the injuries sustained by the deceased establish the guilt of the accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of Accused Nos. 5 and 6 under Section 307 read with Section 34 of the IPC is sustainable.
appellant_arguments: The evidence of P.W.2 cannot be believed due to contradictions between his statement in the FIR and his evidence in court.
P.W.2 did not attribute an individual role to the accused on the day of the incident.
respondent_arguments: The accused were named in the FIR and in the alleged oral declaration by the deceased.
The evidence of the doctor and the injuries sustained by the deceased clearly establish the guilt of the accused.
Merely not attributing a specific overt act to an accused is not fatal to the prosecution's case.
The contradictions in the evidence are very trivial in nature and do not affect the prosecution's case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt. An accused has a right not to be convicted for an offence that is not established by this evidential standard, and the law does not permit a court to convict based on suspicion or a preponderance of probability.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In light of the above discussion, we are in agreement that the case against Accused No. 2 and 3 has not been established beyond reasonable doubt, whereas the same cannot be said with respect to others, whose roles have been proved with cogent evidence available on record. Therefore, while setting aside the conviction and sentence againstAccused Nos. 2 and 3, we maintain the conviction and sentence under Section 302, IPC with respect to Accused A-1 and conviction and sentence under Section 307 read with 34, IPC with respect to accused A-5 and A-6.
legal_tests_applied: The golden thread which passes through out criminal jurisprudence is the standard of “beyond reasonable doubt”.
The prosecution has to prove the guilt of the accused beyond all reasonable doubt.
why_appellant_lost: With respect to Accused Nos. 1, 5, and 6, the court found that their roles have been proved with cogent evidence available on record.
why_respondent_won: With respect to Accused Nos. 1, 5, and 6, the court found that their roles have been proved with cogent evidence available on record.
policy_considerations: Accused has a profound right not to be convicted for an offence which is not established by the evidential standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
The law does not permit the court to convict the accused based on suspicion or on the basis of preponderance of probability.
